title: Geometric realization of a simplicial cylinder
statement:
Let $K$ be any small simplicial set [def-weil-pbc-simplicial-set]. Write $|K|$ for its geometric realization: the quotient of $\coprod_{n\geq0}K_n\times\Delta^n_{\mathrm{top}}$ by $(K(\alpha)x,t)\sim(x,\alpha_*t)$, where $\alpha:[m]\to[n]$ is order preserving, $\Delta^n_{\mathrm{top}}=\{(t_0,\ldots,t_n)\in\mathbf R^{n+1}:t_i\geq0,\ \sum_i t_i=1\}$, and $(\alpha_*t)_j=\sum_{\alpha(i)=j}t_i$. Give this realization its quotient topology, with each $K_n$ discrete. Let $\Delta^1=\operatorname{Hom}_\Delta(-,[1])$, and form $K\times\Delta^1$ degree by degree. The map
$$\rho_K:|K\times\Delta^1|\longrightarrow |K|\times[0,1],\qquad [((x,\theta),t)]\longmapsto\left([x,t],\sum_{\theta(i)=1}t_i\right)$$
is a homeomorphism, natural in $K$. Under this homeomorphism the realizations of the two endpoint inclusions $K\to K\times\Delta^1$ are $u\mapsto(u,0)$ and $u\mapsto(u,1)$, respectively.

source.place: Mark Hovey, Model Categories, Lemma 3.1.8 and its proof, printed pp. 77–78, specialized to the finite simplex Delta[1]. Products with the compact interval have their ordinary product topology. No Stacks tag states this topological realization theorem.

proof.text: By [lem-coef-realization-finite-limits], the quotient realizations in the statement are k-spaces, and the canonical comparison induced by the two projections is a natural homeomorphism $|K\times\Delta^1|\cong |K|\times^{\mathcal K}|\Delta^1|$. The same node says that this k-product is the k-ification of the ordinary product. On representatives the comparison sends $[((x,\theta),t)]$ to $([x,t],[\theta,t])$.

source.place: Lemma 3.1.8 and its proof, printed pp. 77–78 (PDF pages 87–88, counting from 1); k-space limits in Proposition 2.4.22(3), printed p. 58. Only the finite-product and k-space clauses of the cited node are used.

proof.text: Identify $|\Delta^1|$ with $I=[0,1]$ by $e([\theta,t])=\sum_{\theta(i)=1}t_i$. For every monotone $\alpha$, the identity $(\theta\alpha)_*t=\theta_*(\alpha_*t)$ makes this formula invariant under the quotient relations, so it is continuous by continuity on every simplex. Applying the quotient relation to $\theta:[n]\to[1]$ and $\operatorname{id}_{[1]}$ gives $[\theta,t]=[\operatorname{id}_{[1]},\theta_*t]=[\operatorname{id}_{[1]},(1-e([\theta,t]),e([\theta,t]))]$, including constant $\theta$. Thus $s\mapsto[\operatorname{id}_{[1]},(1-s,s)]$ is a continuous two-sided inverse. In particular this identification has the stated coordinate orientation.

source.place: Elementary quotient calculation using the standard topological simplex immediately preceding Lemma 3.1.8, printed p. 77; the coordinate orientation is checked explicitly here.

proof.text: Write $X=|K|$ and $Z=k(X\times I)$ using the k-space topology of [lem-coef-realization-finite-limits]. We prove that the set-theoretic inverse of the continuous identity $Z\to X\times I$ is continuous. Define $G(x)(s)=(x,s)$ as a map $X\to\operatorname{Cont}(I,Z)$, where the mapping space has the compact-open topology of [lem-coef-compact-open-currying]. Each section $I\to Z$ is continuous: it is a continuous map from compact Hausdorff $I$ to the ordinary product, hence to its k-ification by the defining compact-test condition: the inverse image of any k-open set under this compact test is open. For every continuous $a:A\to X$ with $A$ compact Hausdorff, $A\times I$ is compact Hausdorff and $(a,\operatorname{id}_I):A\times I\to X\times I$ is continuous, so it too is continuous into $Z$ by that same inverse-image criterion. To check compactness of $A\times I$ directly, refine an open cover at each $(a,s)$ by product rectangles; compactness of $I$ gives finitely many rectangles covering $\{a\}\times I$, whose first-coordinate neighborhoods have a common intersection $U_a$. These finitely many cover members then cover $U_a\times I$, and compactness of $A$ selects finitely many such $U_a$. Distinct pairs are separated by neighborhoods in a differing coordinate, proving Hausdorffness. The currying clause of [lem-coef-compact-open-currying] makes its transpose $G\circ a$ continuous. Since $X$ has the final compact-test topology, this proves $G$ continuous. The uncurrying clause of the same node, with locally compact source $I$, now makes $(x,s)\mapsto G(x)(s)$ continuous for the ordinary product topology. This is the inverse identity $X\times I\to Z$, as required. Here the interval is compact Hausdorff and locally compact because intersections with sufficiently short closed real intervals form compact neighbourhoods at each point, including its endpoints.

source.place: Agent-written compact-test argument expanding the ordinary-product passage implicit in the discussion after Lemma 3.1.8, printed p. 79, using the locally compact exponential law recalled in Section 2.4, printed p. 49.

proof.text: The interval homeomorphism $e$ of Step 2 induces $1_X\times^{\mathcal K}e$ between the k-products: the product universal property in Step 1 makes it continuous, and $1_X\times^{\mathcal K}e^{-1}$ is its continuous inverse, since their coordinate projections are identities. Compose the homeomorphism in Step 1 with this map and the ordinary-product identification in Step 3. Its formula is exactly $\rho_K([((x,\theta),t)])=([x,t],\sum_{\theta(i)=1}t_i)$. If $f:K\to L$ is simplicial, both orders around the naturality square send this representative to $([f(x),t],\sum_{\theta(i)=1}t_i)$, proving naturality. Under the constant-0 endpoint inclusion the second coordinate is $0$; under the constant-1 inclusion it is $\sum_i t_i=1$. The first coordinate is unchanged, so the endpoint maps are exactly $u\mapsto(u,0)$ and $u\mapsto(u,1)$.
